paras: The killing of Jacob Brooks was the fatal shooting of Brooks, a Black man, by Henry Allen, a special officer at a fertilizer plant, in Alexandria, Virginia, on August 22, 1915. A coroner's jury exonerated Allen the next day, finding that he had fired in self-defense after Brooks, whom he had under arrest, seized his club and attacked him. The Alexandria Gazette counted Brooks as the sixth Black man shot dead by city officers; the only Black-press notice was a brief in the Denver Star weeks later.

Allen worked as a special officer or watchman for the Alexandria Fertilizer and Chemical Company, and two Richmond papers described him as holding "full police power." Brooks was about forty years old, lived at 404 Oronoco Street, had a wife and two children, and worked for the Mutual Ice Company.

According to Allen's testimony at the inquest, he came upon Brooks fighting with a Black woman, named in the papers as Martha Myers, Mayers or Miles, near the chemical plant. Allen said Brooks had knocked the woman down and was kicking her in the side when he intervened and placed both of them under arrest. By his account, a short way up North Lee Street Brooks jerked the hickory baton from his hand and attacked him, and when a blow landed on his head he drew his revolver and fired twice.

The Richmond Virginian placed the shooting on Lee Street between Queen and Princess streets and said the woman threw bricks at Allen during the struggle. It reported that both bullets entered Brooks's right side and that he died almost instantly; in the Herald's account Brooks advanced after the first shot and died minutes after the second. Allen was taken to the Alexandria Hospital, where his head wound was stitched.

Police arrived soon afterward, and the woman was arrested and charged with disorderly conduct and fighting. According to the Richmond Virginian, she admitted at the station that Brooks had been beating her.

City Coroner T. Marshall Jones convened an inquest at Wheatley's undertaking establishment on the morning of August 23. Allen testified first and told the jury he fired because he was afraid his life was in danger. The Gazette said the jury heard "several witnesses," but only Allen's testimony was reported. The jury, with C. J. W. Summers as foreman, found that Allen had fired "in self defense, Brooks having seized his billy and attacked him," and exonerated him. No report of charges against Allen or of any further proceedings was found.

White papers in Alexandria, Washington and Richmond carried the story on August 23 and 24, all on Allen's version. Several headlines presented that version as fact: "Negro Killed While Resisting Officer" in the Washington Times, "Special Officer Shot and Killed Negro Who Was Assaulting Him" in the Alexandria Gazette, and "Watchman Shoots Marauding Negro" in the Richmond Virginian. The Washington Herald and the Richmond Times-Dispatch instead led with the verdict, under "Says He Killed in Self-Defense" and "Watchman Exonerated." On August 25 the Richmond Virginian repeated the Herald's verdict paragraphs inside a report on Alexandria merchants' protest against back taxes.

On August 24 the Gazette ran a short item, "Sunday's Tragedy," observing that the killing "made the sixth member of that race shot to death by officers in this city during past years." It recounted earlier cases going back to 1886, calling the men "desperate" and one officer "forced to shoot," without questioning any of the shootings. The Denver Star's brief of September 11 ran in a news column beside an item about an Illinois sheriff spiriting a prisoner away from a lynch mob. It followed the officer's account, saying Brooks "had words with Martha Myers and had assaulted her" before attacking Allen, and offered no comment.

The versions, all traced to Allen, differ on the sequence. The Gazette and Washington Times had Brooks seize the baton while being led away under arrest, the Richmond Virginian said both prisoners broke away first, and the Herald said Brooks struck Allen when he interfered. They also differ on the woman's surname and on whether Allen received five stitches or four.

reader.title: Killing of Jacob Brooks
bases: A special officer with police powers shot and killed a Black man he said he had under arrest; no crowd was involved (A2, A5, A6).

The local Gazette (A2) and separate Washington and Richmond reports (A1, A4, A5, A6) agree that Allen shot and killed Brooks and was exonerated, though the circumstances come only from Allen's testimony.

accounts.label: Allen's testimony (Washington Herald)
accounts.gist: When Allen interfered in the fight Brooks struck him on the head and arm; he fired, Brooks advanced, he fired again, and Brooks died a few minutes later.

accounts.label: Richmond Virginian report
accounts.gist: Both prisoners broke away; Brooks beat Allen with his walking stick while the woman threw bricks; Brooks died almost instantly; the woman admitted Brooks had been beating her.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Brooks was under arrest and Allen fired in self-defense after Brooks seized his billy and attacked him; Allen exonerated.

accounts.label: Black-press brief
accounts.gist: Brooks had words with and assaulted Martha Myers, attacked Allen when spoken to, and was shot dead.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Negro Killed While Resisting Officer', 'Special Officer Shot and Killed Negro Who Was Assaulting Him' and 'Watchman Shoots Marauding Negro' present Allen's version as fact.
Verdict-led reports ('Says He Killed in Self-Defense', 'Watchman Exonerated') attribute the self-defense claim to Allen and the jury.
The Gazette's 'Sunday's Tragedy' lists six Black men shot by city officers since 1886, calling them 'desperate' and an officer 'forced to shoot'.
The Denver Star ran a two-sentence brief following the officer's account, without comment.
